prompt.context: Our client is a national supermarket chain with $25B in annual sales. The client's sales have been growing at 5% annually compared to 2.5% for the overall market. However, the client projects revenue growth to trend back to market growth rates over the next few years and is looking for ways to boost its profitability. The client has brought BCG in to evaluate one of its options for boosting profits: the introduction of large format grocery stores.
prompt.question: How would you evaluate this opportunity for the client?

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of a typical grocery store?
clarifying_info.a: A typical grocery store is 70,000 square feet.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of a Walmart?
clarifying_info.a: Walmart stores are approximately 200,000 square feet.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of a large format store?
clarifying_info.a: A large format store is 120,000 square feet.

exhibits.title: Large Format vs. Typical Grocery Stores Comparison
exhibits.shows: A table comparing large format stores and typical grocery stores across four dimensions: sales composition by category, monthly revenue, monthly profit, and CapEx required.

large_format_stores.sales_composition: Groceries 50%, Health & beauty products 30%, Personal products 20%

typical_grocery_stores.sales_composition: Groceries 75%, Health & beauty products 15%, Personal products 10%

framework: Benefits of large format stores: higher sales volumes, higher-margin product mix (health & beauty, personal products), potential loyalty/network effects
Costs of large format stores: higher CapEx/leasing requirements for larger footprint, higher inventory sourcing and warehousing costs, potential cannibalization of existing store sales
Comparison metrics: payback period, NPV analysis, return on capital
Alternative strategies to consider: smaller format stores, organic/premium foods push, digital/delivery channels
Cannibalization effects: positive or negative impact on existing store locations

questions.prompt: What can you tell from the exhibit data comparing large format and typical grocery stores?
questions.guidance: Strong answers should observe: (1) Large format store revenues are 50% higher ($960K vs $640K monthly). (2) Large format store profit margins are 10% vs 5% for typical stores — double the margin. (3) The higher margins likely reflect that non-grocery categories (health & beauty, personal products) carry higher margins and represent a larger share of large format sales. (4) Large format stores require nearly double the CapEx ($21M vs $11M). (5) Bonus insight: monthly profits are 3x higher ($96K vs $32K) while CapEx is less than 2x higher — a strong qualitative signal that large format stores are likely the better investment before doing any math.

questions.prompt: How would you compare the two store format options? Calculate and compare the payback periods.
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose NPV or payback period analysis. Payback period = CapEx / Annual Profit. Use monthly profit × 12 to get annual profit. Large format stores have a shorter payback period (~18 years) versus typical stores (~29 years), supporting the large format investment.

math.answer: Large format stores: ~18-year payback; Typical stores: ~29-year payback. Large format stores are a significantly better use of capital.

questions.prompt: What other factors might you need to consider before concluding that large format stores are a good option?
questions.guidance: Candidate should raise cannibalization as a key risk — will large format stores draw customers away from existing store locations? A strong candidate will also mention other factors: competitive response, site availability/real estate constraints, operational complexity, supply chain readiness, customer preferences by market.

questions.prompt: We have data on cannibalization: adding large format stores to areas with existing stores increases sales at existing stores by 2%. What are some reasons why this positive cannibalization might occur?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm using a structured approach. Key insight is network effects: new customers attracted to the large format store may join loyalty programs, which then draws them to existing stores. Other reasons could include: increased brand awareness/visibility in the market, broader product assortment attracting new customer segments who then also use smaller stores for convenience, halo effect on brand perception.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some reasons why adding large format stores might increase (rather than decrease) sales at existing nearby store locations?

categories.name: Network and loyalty effects
ideas: New customers attracted to large format stores join loyalty programs and then patronize existing stores
Cross-shopping: customers use large format for weekly stock-up and nearby stores for convenience trips
Increased brand touchpoints strengthen overall customer relationship

categories.name: Brand and awareness effects
ideas: Larger store acts as a flagship, raising brand visibility and attracting new customers to the overall chain
Positive halo effect: premium large-format experience improves perception of all chain locations

categories.name: Geographic and market effects
ideas: Large format store may draw customers from new geographic areas who then discover nearby existing stores
Cluster effect: multiple locations in an area create convenience network that reinforces repeat visits

categories.name: Operational and supply effects
ideas: Shared supply chain and warehousing for large format store may reduce costs at nearby existing stores
Staff and operational knowledge sharing across formats

recommendation: Recommend that the client introduce large format grocery stores to boost profitability
Large format stores generate higher profit margins (10% vs 5%) on significantly higher revenues ($960K vs $640K monthly)
Large format stores represent a better use of capital with an ~18-year payback period versus ~29 years for typical stores
Large format stores also generate positive cannibalization, increasing sales at existing nearby locations by 2% through network and loyalty effects
risks: High upfront CapEx ($21M per store) requires significant capital commitment
Payback period of ~18 years is long; profitability depends on sustained margin performance
Site availability and real estate constraints may limit rollout pace
Positive cannibalization observed in studies may not generalize to all markets
next_steps: Assess implementation challenges: site selection, construction/leasing timelines, supply chain readiness
Evaluate alternative uses of capital to ensure large format stores represent the best available option
Pilot in select markets before broad rollout to validate financial projections
Analyze competitive landscape to assess risk of rivals entering large format space
